title: Through the AI Fog: The Architectural Decision Agentic Security Depends On — Manoj Nair, Snyk
talk_summary: Snyk's CTO argues that LLM generators cannot reliably validate their own output, citing benchmark data where the latest models found the same vulnerability only ~50% of the time across five runs and hit ~75% recall / 0.40 F1 versus deterministic checks. He also shows that agentic components (skills, MCP servers, packages) are a poisoned, ungoverned attack surface that must be checked deterministically inside the agent loop.

takeaways.technique: Separate generator from validator; keep deterministic checks as the gate
takeaways.what_they_do: They refuse to let the same model that wrote code also judge it, and they pair LLM review with boring deterministic scanners because LLM-only detection is non-deterministic run to run.
takeaways.evidence_quote: run it five times and only 50% of those ones are found across those five tests
takeaways.numbers: ~50% of vulns found across 5 repeated runs; ~75% of issues found by latest models; F1 ~0.40

takeaways.technique: Run each review check N times and measure stability, not single-shot pass
takeaways.what_they_do: They benchmark models by repeating the same detection task five times and reporting how often the issue is caught, exposing run-to-run variance instead of trusting one green result.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We're asking them to find you know the same vulnerability run it five times

takeaways.technique: Deterministic package-health and skill/MCP vetting inside the agent loop
takeaways.what_they_do: Before an agent adopts a dependency or skill, a deterministic tool checks CVE status, maintenance health, and skill contents (e.g. echoing auth headers, pulling instructions from remote YAML); they recommend wiring it as a skill or hook so it is automatic.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we really encourage you to leverage a uh a skill or a hook to make this just a deterministic automated part of your workflow

takeaways.technique: Treat skills/MCP servers as untrusted code requiring review
takeaways.what_they_do: They assess skills and MCP servers for risky behavior (credential exfiltration, remote-controlled logic) before agents use them, since a third of skills were found to contain malware or vulnerabilities.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's actually looking to pull from a YAML file that's hosted on the internet, instructions on how to monitor these targets

takeaways.technique: Route by measured per-task strength, not by model tier
takeaways.what_they_do: Their red-team data shows models trade off by task: frontier models resisted PII extraction but were easier to decision-override, while an open model was the reverse, so they pick per task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the frontier models did worse. The open model 0% of the time you were able to override the decision
takeaways.numbers: 100% PII extraction on one model; 0% decision-override on another

takeaways.technique: OODA-style observe/orient/decide/act loop for agent systems
takeaways.what_they_do: They frame their multi-agent security system as a continuous observe-orient-decide-act loop borrowed from fighter-pilot training, acknowledging multi-agent coordination and shared memory are still unsolved.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you need to really observe, orient, decide and act and that's how you go and in the constant learning from that kind of loop
